summary: 14 finding(s) across 3 file(s): 2 blocker, 3 high, 7 medium, 1 low, 1 info. Availability was judged against QNX 8.0 (no SDP found, unverified). Detected roles: device service, daemon, ipc server. Recommended shape on QNX: a /dev/candaemon resource manager driven by a pulse timer. Readiness score 0/100 (deterministic formula).

findings.title: epoll event loop
findings.guidance: epoll is a Linux-only readiness API. On QNX use POSIX poll()/select() for the lowest-effort port, or restructure the loop around a channel so I/O readiness (ionotify), timers and IPC all arrive as prioritized pulses on one receive call.

alternatives.note: Lowest effort and portable. Keeps the existing loop shape.
One receive loop for I/O readiness, timers and IPC, served in priority order.

findings.sysroot_detail: No SDP index: assumed missing on QNX 8.0 (unverified)

findings.title: SocketCAN
findings.guidance: QNX CAN drivers are resource managers (for example /dev/can1/rx0) controlled through devctl(); the command set depends on the driver for your board. There is no 1:1 SocketCAN replacement. Put CAN access behind a HAL interface and add a QNX backend. Check that a CAN driver exists for your target board first.

alternatives.note: Driver-specific DCMD_* commands on the CAN resource manager.
Generate a CAN HAL interface with a QNX implementation stub.

findings.sysroot_detail: No SDP index: assumed missing on QNX 8.0 (unverified)

findings.title: eventfd notifier
findings.guidance: eventfd is used here as a thread-to-loop wake-up. On QNX a pulse sent to the loop's channel does the same job without a file descriptor, and carries a code and a value. A pipe is the portable fallback.

alternatives.note: Pulses: small, non-blocking, priority-carrying notifications.
Portable fallback; works with poll().

findings.sysroot_detail: No SDP index: assumed missing on QNX 8.0 (unverified)

findings.title: Root-only daemon / Linux capabilities
findings.guidance: QNX splits root's power into abilities. Start as root only long enough to do the privileged setup (for example registering a path name), then call procmgr_ability() to keep just the abilities you need, lock the rest, and switch to an unprivileged user. A secpol policy can express the same thing declaratively.

alternatives.note: Retain only named abilities, then drop root.

findings.title: signalfd
findings.guidance: Block the signals in all threads and handle them in a dedicated thread with sigwaitinfo(), which then notifies the main loop (for example with a pulse).

alternatives.note: Dedicated signal thread; portable.
Signal thread forwards a pulse to the main channel.

findings.sysroot_detail: No SDP index: assumed missing on QNX 8.0 (unverified)

findings.title: Host-only compiler settings
findings.guidance: Cross-compile with qcc/q++ and a -V variant (gcc_ntox86_64, gcc_ntoaarch64le). Remove host-only flags such as -march=native and hardcoded gcc, and do not fail the build when CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME is not Linux. The kit's toolchain file sets all of this.

alternatives.note: cmake/qnx8-toolchain.cmake from the porting kit.

findings.title: fork() in a multithreaded program
findings.guidance: posix_spawn() is the recommended way to start processes on QNX. fork() in a multithreaded program is unsafe under POSIX on any OS, because only the calling thread is copied and locks held by other threads stay locked in the child.

alternatives.note: Create the child in one call; no copy of the parent's address space.

findings.title: ioctl on device descriptors
findings.guidance: QNX offers ioctl() as a wrapper over devctl() for common requests, but driver-specific requests must be rewritten against the QNX driver's DCMD_* set. Wrap device access in a small hardware-abstraction layer (HAL) so the Linux and QNX implementations can live side by side.

alternatives.note: Driver-specific DCMD_* commands; check the driver for your board.
Introduce a HAL interface around device access.

findings.title: Linux-only link libraries
findings.guidance: On QNX the pthread, real-time and dynamic-loading functions are part of libc. Drop a -l flag only if that library is missing from the sysroot (the audit checks this). In CMake prefer find_package(Threads) + Threads::Threads.

alternatives.note: Provided by libc on QNX.

findings.sysroot_detail: No SDP index: assumed missing on QNX 8.0 (unverified)

findings.title: Linux /proc paths
findings.guidance: QNX's /proc is different: per-process information is read with devctl(DCMD_PROC_*) on /proc/<pid>/as. Free memory can be read from the size of /proc itself.

alternatives.note: Query process information through the proc manager.

findings.title: BSD sockets without libsocket

locations.snippet: if (bind(s, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr) < 0) { syslog(LOG_ERR, "bind: %m"); return -1; }

findings.guidance: On QNX the socket API lives in libsocket, not libc. Add -lsocket to the link line and make sure the io-sock network manager runs on the target.

alternatives.note: Link with -lsocket.

findings.sysroot_detail: No SDP index: assumed available on QNX 8.0 (unverified)

findings.title: systemd unit / watchdog script

locations.snippet:
[Unit]
Description=CAN telemetry aggregation daemon
After=sys-subsystem-net-devices-can0.device

[Service]
Type=forking
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/candaemon can0
Restart=on-failure
User=root

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

findings.guidance: QNX targets have no systemd. Start the service from the image's startup script (or SLM where available), and use HAM (High Availability Manager) for restart policies: the service attaches with ham_attach_self() and sends ham_heartbeat(); HAM restarts it when heartbeats stop or it dies. Use only HAM APIs present in your sysroot (several *_control() calls were removed in 8.0.1).

alternatives.note: Heartbeat-based supervision with restart actions.

findings.title: sleep-based periodic loop
findings.guidance: A relative sleep inside a loop drifts by the loop body's run time. Use clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, ...) with a running deadline, or a pulse timer when the thread also needs to receive other events.

alternatives.note: Absolute deadlines remove cumulative drift.
Pulse timer when the loop also receives messages.

findings.title: syslog logging

locations.snippet: if (bind(s, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr) < 0) { syslog(LOG_ERR, "bind: %m"); return -1; }

findings.guidance: syslog() works on QNX. slog2 (slog2_register, slog2f) is recommended for structured, low-overhead logs that you can read with slog2info.

alternatives.note: Ring-buffer logging in shared memory.

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/candaemon.c` multiplexes timers, notifications and I/O in a Linux event loop. A QNX channel replaces it: each source sends a pulse with its own code and priority, and a single receive call hands them to the thread in priority order.
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  TM["timer_create, SIGEV_PULSE"] -->|"code TIMER, prio 30"| CH(("channel"))
  W["worker thread"] -->|"MsgSendPulse, code FLUSH"| CH
  IO["ionotify on fd"] -->|"code IO"| CH
  CH --> L["MsgReceivePulse loop"]

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/candaemon.c` owns a device and a processing loop. On QNX that is naturally a resource manager: it registers /dev/candaemon in the path space, clients use plain open/read/ write/devctl, and every request arrives as a message that inherits the client's priority. Device access moves out of client code into one process that can be restarted on its own.
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C1["client: open + devctl"] -->|"MsgSend, client priority"| R["/dev/candaemon resource manager"]
  T["timer pulse"] --> R
  R --> D["device driver resmgr"]

pillar1_features.rationale: `candaemon.service` runs as root throughout. procmgr_ability() keeps only the abilities the service still needs after start-up and locks the rest before dropping to a service user.
The same least-privilege intent can be written as a secpol policy for candaemon, so the system integrator controls abilities without changing code.
`candaemon.service` relies on systemd or scripts for restarts. HAM supervises the process from outside its address space; with a heartbeat it also catches a hung process, not only a dead one.
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  S["candaemon"] -->|"ham_heartbeat every 0.5 s"| H["HAM"]
  H -->|"missed heartbeats or death"| A["restart action"]
  A --> S

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/candaemon.c` logs through syslog. slog2 gives per-buffer verbosity and very low overhead in time-critical paths, and slog2info reads the buffers on the target.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: The epoll loop treats every ready descriptor equally; a burst on one fd delays the periodic work handled by the same loop.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A channel-based loop receives pulses in priority order, so the control-timer pulse can be given a higher priority than configuration or telemetry events.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: CAN I/O is written directly against the Linux SocketCAN socket family.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A CAN HAL keeps protocol logic portable; the QNX backend talks to the board's CAN resource manager.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: An eventfd wake-up carries no payload and no priority; the receiver must read shared state separately to learn what happened.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A pulse carries an 8-bit code and a 32-bit value plus the sender's priority, so the receiver knows what happened and the scheduler orders the work correctly.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: The process runs with full root privileges for its whole lifetime.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: procmgr_ability() keeps only the abilities the service needs and locks them, so a compromise does not yield root.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Shutdown handling depends on a Linux-only fd type.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A sigwaitinfo() thread is portable and integrates with a pulse-driven loop.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Child processes are created with fork() from a threaded parent.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: posix_spawn() creates the child directly and can set its scheduling policy and priority.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Device control calls are scattered through application code and tied to Linux request codes.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A HAL with a devctl()-based QNX backend isolates board-specific commands in one file.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Restart policy lives in systemd or a cron script, which QNX targets do not have.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Relative sleeps accumulate drift equal to the loop body's execution time.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: Absolute-deadline sleeps or pulse timers keep the period fixed.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Logging goes through syslog, which formats and sends each message to a daemon.

pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: slog2 writes to a shared-memory buffer with per-buffer verbosity, viewable with slog2info.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Device access and client handling live in one process with the application logic.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: As a resource manager the service is a separate process that clients reach through open/read/devctl; it can be restarted without restarting its clients' code. The agent measures the time from spawn until /dev/<service> appears.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Clients exchange data with the service through Linux-specific mechanisms.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: QNX synchronous message passing copies data directly between address spaces and inherits the client's priority. The agent's IPC benchmark measures MsgSend round trips.

pillar3_steps.title: Cross-compile with the QNX 8.0 toolchain
pillar3_steps.explanation: Cross-compile with the kit's toolchain file (qcc/q++ with -V gcc_nto<arch>). Changes needed: Host-only compiler settings: Source qnxsdp-env.sh, then configure with the kit's toolchain file. Linux-only link libraries: Use Threads::Threads and drop -lrt/-ldl where the sysroot has no such library. BSD sockets without libsocket: Add socket to the QNX link libraries.
pillar3_steps.after_code:
# Add to can-telemetry-daemon's CMakeLists.txt after the target "candaemon" is defined:
#   include(cmake/qnx8.cmake)

if(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME STREQUAL "QNX")
  target_compile_definitions(candaemon PRIVATE _QNX_SOURCE)
  target_include_directories(candaemon PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_LIST_DIR}/../include)
  # From the sysroot audit: socket (BSD sockets without libsocket)
  target_link_libraries(candaemon socket)
  # On QNX these functions are normally in libc (unverified: no SDP was indexed):
  #   pthread, rt  -> remove them from target_link_libraries for QNX builds.
endif()

pillar3_steps.title: Replace the epoll loop
pillar3_steps.explanation: Start with poll() so the code builds and runs on QNX. Once it works, consider moving to a channel + pulse loop (see the resource-manager step) where each event source has its own pulse code and priority.

pillar3_steps.title: Introduce a CAN HAL with a QNX backend stub
pillar3_steps.explanation: Define can_hal_open/can_hal_read/can_hal_close. Keep the SocketCAN backend for Linux. The QNX backend opens the CAN driver's device path and uses the driver's devctl commands; fill in the DCMD_* values from the driver you deploy.

pillar3_steps.title: Turn eventfd wake-ups into pulses
pillar3_steps.explanation: Create the notifier with the qnx_compat.h shim from the porting kit. On QNX it sends a pulse to the loop's channel; elsewhere it falls back to a pipe.

pillar3_steps.title: Handle signals in a sigwaitinfo() thread
pillar3_steps.explanation: Block SIGTERM/SIGINT before creating threads, then wait for them in one thread.

pillar3_steps.title: Replace fork()/exec with posix_spawn()
pillar3_steps.explanation: Use posix_spawn(); for daemonizing, let the startup script background the process instead.

pillar3_steps.title: Wrap device control in a HAL
pillar3_steps.explanation: Move ioctl() calls behind functions such as hal_set_line(); implement the QNX side with devctl().

pillar3_steps.title: Replace Linux /proc parsing
pillar3_steps.explanation: Use DCMD_PROC_INFO on /proc/self/as instead of parsing text files.

pillar3_steps.title: Expose the service as a /dev/candaemon resource manager
pillar3_steps.explanation: Start from the kit's resource-manager skeleton. Clients open /dev/candaemon and use read(), write() and devctl() instead of a private socket or shared memory. The periodic work moves into the timer pulse handler, which runs serialized with client requests in one thread.

pillar3_steps.title: Use absolute-deadline sleeps for periodic work
pillar3_steps.explanation: Replace relative sleeps in periodic loops with clock_nanosleep(TIMER_ABSTIME).

pillar3_steps.title: Drop privileges with procmgr_ability()
pillar3_steps.explanation: After privileged setup, allow the specific abilities the service still needs for the non-root domain, deny and lock everything else, then setuid() to a service user.
pillar3_steps.verify_command: pidin -p <service> arg  # on target: confirm non-root uid

pillar3_steps.title: Replace systemd supervision with startup script + HAM
pillar3_steps.explanation: Launch from the image startup script and add a HAM heartbeat.
pillar3_steps.before_code:
[Unit]
Description=CAN telemetry aggregation daemon
After=sys-subsystem-net-devices-can0.device

[Service]
Type=forking
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/candaemon can0
Restart=on-failure
User=root

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

pillar3_steps.title: Optionally switch to slog2
pillar3_steps.explanation: Register a slog2 buffer set at start-up and route log calls through slog2f().

pillar3_steps.title: Build, deploy and verify on a QNX 8.0 target
pillar3_steps.explanation: Build the kit binaries with qcc, boot the QEMU target with mkqnximage, copy the binaries over SSH and run them under the advisor agent, which checks that the resource manager comes up and measures timer and IPC behaviour.

kit.description: CMake toolchain file for qcc/q++ (x86_64, aarch64le)
kit.content:
# QNX SDP 8.0 CMake toolchain file - generated by QNX Integration Advisor for can-telemetry-daemon.
# Usage:
#   source ~/qnx800/qnxsdp-env.sh
#   cmake -B build-qnx -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=cmake/qnx8-toolchain.cmake -DQNX_ARCH=x86_64
#   cmake --build build-qnx

if(NOT DEFINED ENV{QNX_TARGET} OR NOT DEFINED ENV{QNX_HOST})
  message(FATAL_ERROR "QNX_TARGET/QNX_HOST are not set. Source qnxsdp-env.sh from your SDP 8.0 install first.")
endif()

set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME QNX)
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_VERSION 8.0.0)

if(NOT DEFINED QNX_ARCH)
  set(QNX_ARCH x86_64)
endif()

if(QNX_ARCH STREQUAL "x86_64")
  set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR x86_64)
  set(_qnx_variant gcc_ntox86_64)
elseif(QNX_ARCH STREQUAL "aarch64le")
  set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR aarch64)
  set(_qnx_variant gcc_ntoaarch64le)
else()
  message(FATAL_ERROR "Unsupported QNX_ARCH '${QNX_ARCH}' (use x86_64 or aarch64le)")
endif()

# qcc selects the target with -V<variant>; CMake passes COMPILER_TARGET as -V for qcc.
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER qcc)
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_TARGET ${_qnx_variant})
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER q++)
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_TARGET ${_qnx_variant}_cxx)

set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH $ENV{QNX_TARGET} $ENV{QNX_TARGET}/${QNX_ARCH})
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM NEVER)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE ONLY)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PACKAGE ONLY)

# Libraries this repository needs on QNX (from the sysroot audit).
set(QNX_ADVISOR_EXTRA_LIBS socket)

kit.description: Only the compatibility shims this repo needs
Resource manager skeleton at /dev/candaemon (dispatch/iofunc, pulse timer, procmgr_ability)
Runs every shim in qnx_compat.h on the target
Builds the kit binaries with qcc
kit.content:
# Builds the QNX porting-kit binaries for can-telemetry-daemon.
#   source ~/qnx800/qnxsdp-env.sh && make -f Makefile.qnx ARCH=x86_64
ARCH ?= x86_64
VARIANT_x86_64    = gcc_ntox86_64
VARIANT_aarch64le = gcc_ntoaarch64le
CC      = qcc -V$(VARIANT_$(ARCH))
CFLAGS  = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=gnu11 -Iinclude -Isrc
OUT     = build/$(ARCH)

all: $(OUT)/candaemon_resmgr $(OUT)/candaemonctl $(OUT)/compat_selftest

$(OUT)/candaemon_resmgr: src/qnx_candaemon_resmgr.c src/candaemon_dcmd.h
	mkdir -p $(OUT)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $<

$(OUT)/candaemonctl: src/candaemonctl.c src/candaemon_dcmd.h
	mkdir -p $(OUT)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $<

$(OUT)/compat_selftest: tests/compat_selftest.c include/qnx_compat.h
	mkdir -p $(OUT)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $<

clean:
	rm -rf build

.PHONY: all clean

kit.description: mkqnximage QEMU target + copy binaries over SSH
kit.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Build and boot a QNX 8.0 QEMU target with mkqnximage, then copy the kit binaries to it.
# Generated by QNX Integration Advisor for can-telemetry-daemon.
# Prerequisites: QNX SDP 8.0 with mkqnximage, QEMU, `source qnxsdp-env.sh`, an SSH key.
# Check `mkqnximage --help` for the exact options in your SDP patch level.
set -eu

ARCH=${ARCH:-x86_64}
VM_DIR=${VM_DIR:-$HOME/qnx-advisor-vm}
SSH_PUB=${SSH_PUB:-$HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub}
KIT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)

command -v mkqnximage >/dev/null || { echo "mkqnximage not found: source qnxsdp-env.sh first" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$SSH_PUB" ] || { echo "SSH public key $SSH_PUB not found (set SSH_PUB)" >&2; exit 1; }

mkdir -p "$VM_DIR"
cd "$VM_DIR"
if [ ! -d output ]; then
    echo "== building QEMU image in $VM_DIR"
    mkqnximage --type=qemu --arch="$ARCH" --ssh-ident="$SSH_PUB"
fi

echo "== starting VM (headless)"
mkqnximage --run=-h &
sleep 5

IP=""
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
    IP=$(mkqnximage --getip 2>/dev/null || true)
    [ -n "$IP" ] && break
    sleep 2
done
[ -n "$IP" ] || { echo "could not get VM IP" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "== VM at $IP"

make -C "$KIT_DIR" -f Makefile.qnx ARCH="$ARCH"
scp -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new "$KIT_DIR"/build/"$ARCH"/* qnxuser@"$IP":/data/home/qnxuser/
echo "== copied kit binaries to /data/home/qnxuser on $IP"
echo "   ssh qnxuser@$IP"
echo "   then: su -c '/data/home/qnxuser/candaemon_resmgr -u 1000 &' && /data/home/qnxuser/candaemonctl"

# Advanced / optional: mkifs buildfile fragment for can-telemetry-daemon.
# For QEMU and VMs prefer mkqnximage (target/run-qemu.sh). Merge this fragment into a
# board buildfile from your BSP if you build a custom image.

[+script] .candaemon-start = {
    /proc/boot/candaemon_resmgr -p 100 -u 1000 &
    waitfor /dev/candaemon 5
}

[perms=0755] /proc/boot/candaemon_resmgr = build/x86_64/candaemon_resmgr
[perms=0755] /proc/boot/candaemonctl = build/x86_64/candaemonctl
